section_summary: This section is dominated by Seattle-area church petitions and citizen protests urging the United States to prohibit exports of scrap iron, munitions, oil, cotton, and other strategic materials to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. It also contains diplomatic and consular reporting on British and Italian arms exports, Japanese use of cotton waste in explosives, and Japanese military purchases of foreign trucks. Later correspondence records public appeals from Virginia, Michigan, California, and Tennessee and State Department replies explaining that the Neutrality Act did not authorize an embargo on raw materials and had not been invoked against China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Unidentified petition signature sheet
subfiles.from: Unidentified petition signers
subfiles.about: A fragmentary concluding signature sheet from an anti-war-materials petition.
subfiles.summary: Petition signature sheet with poorly legible names and addresses, including a reverend and several Seattle-area signers.

subfiles.title: Alki Community Church petition against exports to aggressor nations
subfiles.from: Members and friends of Alki Community Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Seattle church members ask Congress and the executive branch to prohibit shipments of scrap iron and munitions to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: Alki Community Church petition, on Rev. David Nourse's stationery, urges quick legislation against scrap iron and munitions exports to aggressor nations, followed by signers.

subfiles.title: Crown Hill Methodist Episcopal Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Crown Hill Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: The congregation appeals for legislation banning scrap-iron and munitions shipments to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: Three signature sheets repeat the same appeal on Crown Hill Methodist Episcopal Church stationery. Wayne L. Sprague is identified as minister, and the pages contain numerous congregational signatures and Seattle addresses.

subfiles.title: Seattle First Baptist Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Seattle First Baptist Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: First Baptist congregants request legislation prohibiting scrap-iron and munitions exports to aggressors.
subfiles.summary: Two lightly populated signature sheets carry the standard Seattle church appeal. The OCR preserves few legible names, but the petition language clearly calls for federal export restrictions.

subfiles.title: First Methodist Episcopal Church petition and signature sheets
subfiles.from: Members of First Methodist Episcopal Church, Seattle
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: A large group of Methodist congregants petitions for a ban on scrap-iron and munitions shipments to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: The opening and repeated headings state the standard appeal for federal legislation. Eleven further pages consist principally of handwritten names and Seattle addresses, many poorly recognized by OCR.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Woodland Park Methodist Church petitions
subfiles.from: N. Ekohr
subfiles.about: The writer forwards petitions signed at Woodland Park Methodist Church.
subfiles.summary: N. Ekohr tells Hiltner petitions signed at Woodland Park Methodist Church that morning are enclosed, calling the campaign worthwhile.

subfiles.title: Seattle protest against scrap-iron shipment at East Waterway Dock
subfiles.from: Seattle citizens and the Committee Against International Aggression
subfiles.to: Dulien Steel Products Corporation; East Waterway Dock Company
subfiles.about: Seattle citizens protest scrap-iron exports to Japan and a shipment then being loaded at East Waterway Dock.
subfiles.summary: The petition argues that scrap iron should not be sent to Japan while it is conducting aggressive war in China. It specifically objects to a shipment being loaded by the named companies and carries signatures and addresses on two pages.

subfiles.title: Circular to Seattle pastors requesting petition signatures
subfiles.from: Walter G. Hiltner, Committee Against International Aggression
subfiles.about: Hiltner asks churches to circulate a standard resolution against exports of scrap iron and munitions.
subfiles.summary: Hiltner reports church, business and labor representatives adopted the resolution, asks Seattle pastors to gather signatures Sunday for President Roosevelt, and announces an April 12 YWCA committee meeting.

subfiles.title: Salem Evangelical Free Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Salem Evangelical Free Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Church members appeal for legislation prohibiting scrap-iron and munitions shipments to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: The petition appears on stationery naming K. P. Wuflestad as pastor. Two pages contain the standard resolution and congregants' names and addresses.

subfiles.title: Queen Anne Methodist Episcopal Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Queen Anne Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: The Queen Anne congregation requests legislation against scrap-iron and munitions exports.
subfiles.summary: The petition names William C. Bowman as minister and reproduces the standard Committee Against International Aggression appeal. The two pages are largely occupied by signatures and addresses.

subfiles.title: West Seattle Christian Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of West Seattle Christian Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: West Seattle congregants call for a prohibition on shipments of scrap iron and munitions to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: Five pages on church stationery identify C. M. Ridenour as minister and repeat the standard legislative appeal. Most of the document consists of numbered or handwritten signatures and West Seattle addresses.

subfiles.title: Committee circular with attached Queen Anne-area signature sheets
subfiles.from: Walter G. Hiltner, Committee Against International Aggression
subfiles.about: A copy of Hiltner's church circular is followed by petition signatures, chiefly from the Queen Anne area.
subfiles.summary: The circular repeats the request that pastors gather signatures for an embargo resolution and return them for transmission to President Roosevelt. Two appended pages list signers and addresses but do not clearly identify the participating church.

subfiles.title: Christ Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Christ Church, Seattle
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Christ Church members support legislation prohibiting exports of scrap iron and munitions to aggressors.
subfiles.summary: The petition is printed on Christ Church stationery naming Rector Paul Boynton James and Honorary Associate Herbert Henry Gowen. Three pages contain the standard appeal and congregants' names and addresses.

subfiles.title: Dunlap Baptist Church petition
subfiles.from: Members and congregation of Dunlap Baptist Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Dunlap Baptist congregants petition for legislation banning scrap-iron and munitions exports to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: The first page contains the full standard appeal followed by names and addresses. A second page continues the list of Seattle signers.

subfiles.title: Asbury Methodist Episcopal Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Asbury Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Asbury Methodist congregants appeal for legislation stopping shipments of scrap iron and munitions to aggressors.
subfiles.summary: The petition identifies P. Malcolm Hammond as pastor and gives the standard Seattle church resolution. Page 104 is marked as a duplicate page two and contains an additional long list of signers.

subfiles.title: Plymouth Church Easter telephone message
subfiles.from: Plymouth Church
subfiles.about: A church message invites members to an Easter communion service and urges support for an emergency Easter offering.
subfiles.summary: Plymouth Church Easter telephone message asks members to a Thursday communion service Dr. Fifield thinks significant and reminds them of an Easter offering.

subfiles.title: Woodland Park Methodist Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Woodland Park Methodist Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States; Department of State; Senate; House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Woodland Park Methodist congregants call for legislation banning scrap-iron and munitions exports to aggressors.
subfiles.summary: The first page states the standard appeal and begins a list of signers. Two more pages continue the names and addresses, although much of the handwriting is poorly captured by OCR.

subfiles.title: Japanese industry and the mixture of staple fiber with cotton cloth
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul
subfiles.about: The consul reports that rayon or wood staple fiber mixed with Japanese cotton cloth is creating difficulties in explosives manufacture and railway use.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese chemical source reportedly said machinery for converting cotton waste to nitrocellulose can't process wood fiber in mixed cloth, impairing nitrate products, though a workable process is expected; mixed waste was also unsuitable as locomotive gearbox packing.

subfiles.title: Exports of British war material to Japan
subfiles.from: Herschel V. Johnson, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: The embassy transmits a British parliamentary exchange concerning arms-export licenses and shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hansard: Britain issued eight war-material export licenses to Japan since July 1, 1937, consigning £61,000 of arms and stores through February 28, 1938; Captain Wallace cites the 1911 treaty, while Riley and Noel-Baker object.

subfiles.title: Instruction requesting report on unrecorded Japanese military imports
subfiles.from: Department of State, signed by Acting Secretary Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: The Department requests analysis of Japanese military imports omitted from official statistics.
subfiles.summary: Telegram cites Kobe despatch 235 of March 17 and asks Tokyo to discuss the level and trend of unrecorded Japanese military imports compared with before the conflict.

subfiles.title: Sale of equipment and ammunition by Italy to Japan
subfiles.doc_type: diplomatic despatch with military attaché report
subfiles.from: William Phillips, United States Ambassador in Italy; enclosure by Col. G. H. Paine
subfiles.about: The embassy reports Italian aircraft, ammunition, and possible aviation personnel supplied to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Phillips forwards an attache report: serial numbers suggest 112 Breda Ba.20 aircraft shipped to Japan, artillery shells made for a Japanese order, and Italian aviation personnel in East Asia probably instructional or civilian.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on British export figures
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: An internal note observes that London's latest figures duplicate those in an earlier despatch.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs notes London despatch 219 of April 21 quotes the same export figures as before.

subfiles.title: Exports of British war material to China and Japan
subfiles.from: Herschel V. Johnson, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: The London embassy transmits comparative British arms-export figures for China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The despatch quotes Hansard as reporting nineteen export licenses for China and eight for Japan since July 1, 1937. Registered British arms and military-store exports through February 28, 1938, totaled £183,000 for China and £61,000 for Japan. It notes that the Japanese figures match those sent in the earlier despatch.

subfiles.title: Richmond Methodist appeal against materials for Japanese war munitions
subfiles.from: Members of Monument Methodist Episcopal Church, South, Richmond
subfiles.about: A Richmond congregation asks the government to stop materials used to manufacture Japanese war munitions.
subfiles.summary: The poorly reproduced letter states that a congregation of about 190 members unanimously requested action against shipments to Japan. It invokes the suffering of a defenseless nation and appeals in religious language for an end to the slaughter. Several pages appear to repeat portions of the same handwritten text.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Fred H. Townsend's letter on the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Andrew J. Transue, Member of Congress
subfiles.about: Transue forwards a constituent's views on the Neutrality Act for a State Department response.
subfiles.summary: Congressman forwards Rev. Fred Townsend's Davison, Michigan letter on the Neutrality Act and asks Hull to answer him directly.

subfiles.title: Fred H. Townsend's appeal for an embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: Fred H. Townsend
subfiles.about: A retired Methodist minister urges an embargo on scrap iron, raw cotton, and oil exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Townsend, a retired Methodist minister, urges the President to invoke the Neutrality Act to help end Japan's undeclared war and killing of noncombatants.

subfiles.title: Reply to Andrew J. Transue concerning Townsend's letter
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Transue's referral and sends a copy of the Department's reply to Townsend.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Andrew Transue Townsend's questions concern the Neutrality Act and scrap, cotton and oil exports, enclosing the direct reply and returning Townsend's letter.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Fred H. Townsend
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked and why it could not block raw-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Townsend a war finding would bar arms to both China and Japan, no statute authorizes an embargo on scrap, cotton or oil, and the President judged invoking it would not serve overall interests.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence attaché report form concerning exports
subfiles.from: Unidentified naval attaché
subfiles.about: A badly degraded attaché report records military material reportedly received for export.
subfiles.summary: Naval Intelligence attache-report form, mostly illegible, apparently on military items or ammunition received for export.

subfiles.title: Pasadena petition to stop strategic-material shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Torrance Phelps and other Pasadena residents
subfiles.about: Pasadena residents ask the President to stop shipments of scrap iron, crude oil, and raw cotton used by Japan in the war against China.
subfiles.summary: The letter asks Roosevelt to halt exports that enable Japan to wage war on China and states that the signers favor immediately stopping the shipments. The opening or concluding wording is duplicated or out of order on page 130. Page 132 contains an extended list of Pasadena-area signers and addresses.

subfiles.title: Reply to Torrance Phelps on raw-material exports
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that the Neutrality Act does not permit the President to embargo scrap iron, crude oil, or raw cotton.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that the 1937 act authorizes restrictions on arms, ammunition, and implements of war but expressly excludes the raw materials named by Phelps. He says no other statute supplies the requested authority. Copies of the Neutrality Act and the pamphlet International Traffic in Arms are enclosed.

subfiles.title: Japanese military purchases of foreign trucks
subfiles.from: Richard W. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Boyce summarizes heavy Japanese military purchases of American and German trucks.
subfiles.summary: Consul reports a $400,000 Chrysler and White truck sale for Japanese forces in Manchukuo, continuing Ford purchases, a Mukden firm ordering 800-1,000 Diamond T trucks, and tires for 1,000 Dodge and 1,000 Mercedes trucks.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting Methodist General Conference resolutions
subfiles.from: Lud H. Estes, Secretary, General Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South
subfiles.about: Estes transmits resolutions adopted by the church's quadrennial General Conference.
subfiles.summary: Estes officially conveys resolutions of the Methodist General Conference, closing in Birmingham, with a religious expression of support for Hull.

subfiles.title: Methodist Episcopal Church, South resolution on aid to Japan
subfiles.from: General Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: The church calls for measures preventing American material or financial resources from aiding Japan's war against China.
subfiles.summary: Methodist Episcopal Church, South resolution, adopted at Birmingham April 30, 1938, asks the President and Congress to stop government or private resources from aiding Japan's invasion of China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Lud H. Estes
subfiles.from: B. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds to the Methodist resolution by explaining the Neutrality Act and reporting arms-license totals for China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Moore tells Estes a war proclamation would bar arms to both China and Japan, the law doesn't authorize other restrictions, and licenses since July 1, 1937 were $12,340,580.81 for China and $7,496,490.28 for Japan.

subfiles.title: Fred H. Townsend's rebuttal to the State Department
subfiles.from: Fred H. Townsend
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Townsend denounces the Department's Neutrality Act explanation and renews his call to cut off strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Townsend calls the reply evasion, argues Japan's aggression is plainly war, attacks reliance on presidential discretion, says scrap, cotton and oil are war implements, and urges relief for China and measures weakening Japan.
